description: The classical Jyotish texts and Samudrika Shastra: what each covers, where it comes from, and where to read the originals. Described, never reproduced.

translations.en: The BPHS is the core text of what is now called Parashari Jyotish. It sets out the zodiac and its divisions, the grahas and their natures, the twelve bhavas, aspects, yogas, the Vimshottari dasha, the divisional charts (vargas) and longevity.

items.bodh_3to4line: Almost every modern Jyotish practice - including the dasha system and the varga charts this site computes - traces back to it. The attribution to Parashara is traditional; the text as we have it was compiled and expanded over centuries. Source: the Sanskrit text is public domain. Several early English translations exist; check each translator's date before reusing any of them.

translations.en: Varahamihira's Brihat Jataka is among the earliest surviving systematic works of Indian horoscopy, written in a compact verse style. It treats the signs, the grahas, the bhavas, and the results of planetary combinations.

translations.en: Attributed to Jaimini, these sutras set out a distinct method: the chara karakas (the grahas ranked by degree as signifiers of self, spouse, career and so on), argala and virodhargala, and the rashi dashas, rather than the Parashari bhava-and-dasha approach.

translations.en: The Brihat Samhita is not a text of natal astrology. It is an encyclopaedic work on omens, the transits of the grahas, weather and rain, agriculture, architecture, gems, and - in the chapters that matter here - the marks on the human body.

items.bodh_3to4line: Because it ranges so widely it is the single richest early source for samudrika shastra in Sanskrit. Source: public domain; 6th century CE.

translations.en: Samudrika Shastra is the branch of Jyotish that reads the human body - its build, complexion, voice, gait, the marks and lines on the skin, and the form of the hands and feet - and draws conclusions from them about a person's past and future.

items.summary_1line: The Indian tradition of reading the body
items.summary_2to3line: Samudrika Shastra is the branch of Jyotish that reads the human body - its build, complexion, voice, gait, the marks and lines on the skin, and the form of the hands and feet - and draws conclusions from them about a person's past and future.
items.bodh_3to4line: The name comes from Samudra, understood both as a name of Shiva and as a sage, and the body itself is called samudra because it is 'imprinted with lines'. Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita treats it in the chapters on the marks of men, of the great man, and of women (67, 69 and 70 in the vulgate numbering; 68, 70 and 71 in editions that count an extra chapter). Source: Brihat Samhita, public domain.

translations.en: Brihat Samhita opens its chapter on the marks of men by saying that a learned person should first examine twelve things: the body, the complexion, the voice, the strength, the joints, the gloss, the colour, the shape of the face, the height, the weight, the disposition, and the gait - and only then speak.

items.bodh_3to4line: That ordering is worth noticing. The text puts measurement and observation before interpretation, and later verses give actual proportions - the navel at the mid-point of the body, the circumference of the head equal to the waist, the nose the length of the forefinger. Source: Brihat Samhita, chapter on the marks of men.

translations.en: Brihat Samhita describes the lines of the palm directly. The line running from the root of the thumb toward the root of the first finger is called the Male line and stands for the man himself; the line next to it stands for his partner. If the two join between the thumb and the first finger, the text reads long conjugal happiness; if they are separated, the couple stay apart.

items.bodh_3to4line: It names a line running from the foot of the little finger to that of the forefinger as the Life line, and a vertical line from the wrist toward the root of the second finger as the Fortune or wealth line. A cut or defect in a line is read as ill health or danger. It also holds that a person's left palm indicates the spouse's fortune and the right their own - and the reverse for a woman. Source: Brihat Samhita, chapter on the marks of men.

translations.en: Brihat Samhita gives a set of marks found on the body and the palm and assigns each to a graha: a circle to the Sun, a square to the Moon, a triangle to Mars, an arrow to Mercury, and further shapes - a quadrilateral, a pentagon, a bow, a flag - to the remaining grahas.

items.bodh_3to4line: The method that follows is genuinely astrological: find the limb the mark sits on, and the nakshatra and sign assigned to that limb, and you have the graha's position at the person's birth. The text also gives a way to work out the natal ascendant from body measurements - height and head circumference. Source: Brihat Samhita, chapter on the marks of men. This is a description of what the text says, not a claim that it works.

translations.en: Later samudrika literature divides the subject into three branches: palmistry, the reading of the body and face, and the marks of women. It also sorts marks into three kinds - natural, seasonal or temporal, and casual - and holds that the lines are the writing of the creator on the body, which an expert can read.

items.bodh_3to4line: The Brihat Samhita gives a separate chapter to the marks of women, and the Garudapurana redacts the same material into its own chapters on men's and women's marks. Source: Brihat Samhita and the Garudapurana; both public domain. The Puranic version is an abbreviated redaction, so where the two differ the Samhita is the fuller text.

translations.en: Samudrika Shastra is a traditional system of interpretation with no demonstrated predictive validity, and nothing here is offered as a reading of your own body. The Brihat Samhita's own verses run from careful proportion to claims about a man's fate from the number of hairs in a pore; the two are not the same kind of statement.

items.bodh_3to4line: The site presents this material because it is the authentic Indian source for palmistry and body reading, and because it is public domain and therefore quotable in description. It is not a diagnostic tool and not a basis for decisions. Source: Brihat Samhita; described, not reproduced.

translations.en: The Sanskrit originals of all these texts are public domain. The trouble is translations: the well-known modern ones - Santhanam, Sagar, Ranjan and others - are still in copyright, so they cannot be reused. Older English renderings from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries usually are free.
